lesson.title: THD: Putting a Single Number on Distortion
lesson.summary: Total harmonic distortion, or THD, combines every harmonic a circuit generates into one percentage figure, and it is the standard way distortion is specified on datasheets and measured on test equipment.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter looked at one harmonic at a time. A real nonlinear circuit usually generates several harmonics simultaneously, at different levels, so describing its distortion fully would mean listing every single one. Total harmonic distortion, THD, solves that by combining the whole series into one number.

Because the different harmonics sit at different frequencies, they behave as uncorrelated, independent contributors, so their powers add rather than their voltages adding directly. That means THD is computed as a root sum of squares: THD = sqrt(V2 squared plus V3 squared plus V4 squared, and so on) divided by V1, the fundamental's amplitude, then multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage. THD can also be expressed in decibels using the same 20 times log10 form used throughout this sequence, applied to the ratio before converting to a percentage, connecting directly back to the general decibel concept.

Here is a worked example, extending the previous chapter's numbers. Take a fundamental V1 of 1 V, a second harmonic V2 of 0.02 V, a third harmonic V3 of 0.01 V, and a fourth harmonic V4 of 0.005 V. First square each harmonic: 0.02 squared is 0.0004, 0.01 squared is 0.0001, and 0.005 squared is 0.000025. Add them: 0.0004 plus 0.0001 plus 0.000025 equals 0.000525. Take the square root: sqrt(0.000525) is about 0.02291. Divide by the fundamental, 1 V, which changes nothing here, and multiply by 100 to get a percentage: THD is about 2.29 percent. Converting that same ratio to decibels: 20 times log10(0.02291) is about 20 times negative 1.640, or about negative 32.8 dB.

Notice that the single second harmonic alone, from the previous chapter, measured about 2 percent, or negative 33.98 dB. Once the third and fourth harmonics are folded in, THD rises slightly to 2.29 percent, or negative 32.8 dB, a larger, less negative figure, because those additional harmonics each add a little more distortion power even though individually they are smaller than the second harmonic. High quality audio electronics are often specified at well under 0.1 percent THD, while a cheap, poorly designed, or overdriven circuit can reach several percent or more. As the headroom chapter suggested, one of the most common real world causes of a sudden jump in THD is a signal running out of headroom and starting to clip, a topic covered later in this sequence.
